title: Summer ozone did not make autumn leaf colouring or leaf fall clearly earlier in Germany and Switzerland in 1990-2023 or at US PhenoCam sites in 2007-2023 after weather control
abstract: We tested whether growing-season ground-level ozone makes autumn leaf senescence of deciduous trees earlier, as chamber and FACE experiments suggest. We used three observation systems: DWD observers in Germany (beech, oak, birch; 123,081 colouring records at 7,129 station-species units, 1990-2023), MeteoSwiss observers in Switzerland (beech, birch; 5,462 records), and US PhenoCam canopy cameras (280 site-years at 32 sites, 2007-2023). Exposure was the May-August mean daily maximum 8-hour ozone from 432 German and 34 Swiss EEA monitors and EPA AQS monitors, as anomalies from a monitor-offset model, interpolated within 50 km (US 75 km). Models had station-species and species-year fixed effects, seasonal temperature, water balance and radiation terms, and two-way clustered errors. We wrote the plan, two placebo tests and a decision rule first. Germany gave +0.37 days per 10 ppb (95% CI -0.01 to +0.76) for colouring and +0.08 (-0.43 to +0.58) for leaf fall. Switzerland gave -1.31 (-4.34 to +1.72) and the US -2.30 (-11.51 to +6.91). The hypothesis failed the decision rule. In Germany both placebos (spring leaf unfolding; next-year ozone) gave about -0.5 days per 10 ppb with intervals below zero, so residual confounding of this size remains. If bias is not larger than this, a true advance of more than about 0.6 days per 10 ppb in Germany is not compatible with the data. Limitations: after fixed effects the usable ozone variation is only about 2 ppb, so the 10 ppb scale is an extrapolation; ozone co-varies with heat; monitors are 12-20 km from stations; human observers change; the Swiss and US samples are small.
